title: AI Toxicity Predictions Overstated: New Benchmark Exposes Hidden Data Leakage
key_facts: Gachon University (South Korea) built ToxBench, a benchmark auditing how toxicity-prediction models are tested; published in BMC Bioinformatics.
Uses Tox21 (7,538 compounds, 12 endpoints), ClinTox (1,379 compounds) and SIDER (1,350 compounds, 27 tasks).
Four model types, random versus scaffold-based splits, five seeds, 120 conditions.
On Tox21, moving to scaffold splitting cut AUROC by 0.057 to 0.079 points (mean 0.070) across all four models.
Test compounds with close similarity (above 0.6) to training data fell from 43.9% to 12.1% with scaffold splitting.
ClinTox results were dominated by sampling noise (plus or minus 0.085 to 0.160 AUROC).
Scaffold splitting worsened probability calibration on all three datasets.
quote_evidence: The study, published in BMC Bioinformatics, quantifies exactly how much performance drops when structurally similar molecules are kept out of the test set.

Moving from random to scaffold splitting reduced the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, or AUROC, by 0.057 to 0.079 points across all four model classes on Tox21, with a mean drop of 0.070.
ClinTox, the smallest of the three, showed a reversed performance ordering between split types.
why_it_matters_hint: Drug-safety predictions are only as credible as the way they were tested.
event_date: Study published in BMC Bioinformatics; article dated 5 Oct 2026
notes: Article carries Scienmag's text (credited at the end); Scienmag is named as source. Score kept at 5.
